item.title: Parallel Circuit Execution for Scalable Quantum Computation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Parallel circuit execution on 156-qubit ibm_boston processor reduces billed QPU execution time by 3.5×--5.5× while retaining 83--92% of sequential fidelity.

Grade 0.377 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Avimita Chatterjee, W. Michael Brown, Siyuan Niu, Wibe Albert de Jong, Thomas Lubinski

Figure

Hellinger fidelity and billed QPU execution time on ibm_boston plotted against circuit qubit width. Parallel execution achieves 3.5×--5.5× runtime reductions while closely matching sequential fidelity across benchmarks.

Asks

How can idle qubits on large quantum processors be utilized to execute multiple independent circuits simultaneously and reduce execution time?

Before

Qiskit ParallelExperiment provided multi-circuit execution mechanics but required manual partition selection without error awareness.

But

Dependent on availability of low-error disjoint device partitions and prone to transpiler escape constraints; multi-GPU classical scaling evaluated up to 28 qubits and 16 GPUs.

Tools

IBM 156-qubit ibm_boston processor · CUDA-Q and MPI on NERSC Perlmutter · QED-C application-oriented benchmarks · Topology-aware greedy partition mapping algorithm

Abstract

Today's quantum processors have tens to hundreds of physical qubits, but reliable execution of arbitrary circuits remains limited to fewer than 30 entangled qubits across hardware modalities. Building upon prior work, we introduce an error- and topology-aware method for mapping multiple independent circuits onto disjoint regions of a single large-scale QPU for parallel circuit execution. For applications with many similarly sized circuits, such as observable estimation for Hamiltonian simulation, this approach can reduce billed QPU execution time, with ideal speedup proportional to the number of usable partitions. We demonstrate the approach on IBM's 156-qubit ibm_boston processor using standard QED-C benchmark and Hamiltonian-based observable-estimation workloads. Compared with standard sequential execution, parallel execution reduces billed execution time by 3.5-5.5x while retaining 83-92% of the sequential fidelity. We further evaluate the scaling of parallel circuit execution using GPU-accelerated classical simulation, distributing measurement circuits across GPUs via MPI. Using CUDA-Q on the NERSC Perlmutter system, we achieve up to 13.8x speedup on 16 GPUs (86% parallel efficiency) for an H2 electronic-structure simulation, with scaling evaluated across multiple Hamiltonians and circuit counts. These results provide an indication of the performance ceiling that parallel execution on future quantum hardware may eventually approach. Both execution modes are implemented as a runtime option within the QED-C Application-Oriented Benchmark suite. Together, the results show that circuit-level parallelism can reduce execution cost on current quantum hardware and simulation time on GPU clusters, with the potential for greater benefits as device quality and qubit counts increase.

item.title: Benchmarking the computational power of quantum computers
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Defines QUOPS to benchmark quantum capability by circuit size and execution rate. Translating utility challenge problems (factoring RSA-2048, FeMoco) shows computational capability must grow by 5 orders of magnitude over current physical processors (Quantinuum Helios-1 Q=1504, H2-1 Q=1320).

Grade 0.366 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Timothy Proctor, Oliver Hart, Oliver Widzowski Maupin, Matthew Girling, Daniel Hothem, Daniel Mills, Jordan Hines, Karl Mayer, Jacob S. Nelson, Tyler LeBlond, Zohim Chandani, Diego Forlivesi, Piper C. Wysocki, Boldizsár Poór, Joan M. Dreiling, Annie Park, Adam P. Reed, Brian Estey, Cameron Foltz, Akhil Isanaka, M. S. Allman, Michael Mills, Maxwell D. Urmey, Peter E. Siegfried, Audrey Faricy, Jin-Sung Kim, Cristina Cîrstoiu, Andrew D. Baczewski, Charles H. Baldwin, Robin Blume-Kohout

Figure

Plots QUOPS capability regions (circuit size vs width), historical capability score scaling vs time with exponential trend lines showing 1.4-year (Quantinuum) and 2.1-year (IBM) doubling times, and QUOPS execution rate vs score for physical, logical, and projected architectures against utility milestones.

Asks

How can quantum computational power be directly benchmarked and compared across disparate physical and logical architectures relative to utility-scale challenge problems?

Before

Quantum volume and physical gate error rates; quantum volume scaling requires exponential classical verification and does not map directly to fault-tolerant utility resource requirements.

But

Historical score inferences rely on global depolarizing noise, two-qubit gates as the sole error source, and simplified compilation models accurate to within roughly a factor of two.

Tools

QUOPS benchmark suite · Mirror circuit fidelity estimation · Steane llbracket7,1,3rrbracket logical processor · Quantinuum Helios-1 ion-trap processor · IBM ibm_boston and Google Willow superconducting processors

Abstract

Quantum computing hardware is advancing rapidly toward utility-scale machines that will enable scientific breakthroughs. Many teams are pursuing distinct and difficult-to-compare routes to this goal, using different qubit technologies and logical architectures. Tracking progress toward quantum utility therefore requires rigorous benchmarks that measure computational capability relative to utility-scale challenge problems and enable fair comparison across disparate platforms. Here we demonstrate direct, cross-platform measurement of quantum computational capability using a new benchmark that quantifies the size of the largest computationally relevant quantum circuits that a machine can execute successfully and the speed at which it can execute them. We apply this quantum universal operation performance system (QUOPS) experimentally to leading processors from Quantinuum, Google, and IBM, computing directly on physical qubits. Translating state-of-the-art resource requirements for recognized challenge problems that represent useful quantum computation into effective QUOPS circuit sizes shows that computational capability must grow by 5 orders of magnitude, motivating fault-tolerant approaches. We use the same benchmark to assess the performance of a simple fault-tolerant logical-qubit processor implemented on up to eight [[7,1,3]]-encoded logical qubits using Quantinuum Helios-1, and project the growth of capability across successive generations of fault-tolerant quantum computers to show how QUOPS can track progress toward quantum scientific utility.

item.title: State-adapted generalized mean-field projections for Pauli propagation of Heisenberg dynamics
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Covariance-orthogonal projection πmσ0 compresses Heisenberg observables onto at-most-m-body subspaces while preserving expectation values ⟨𝐎⟩σ0 and spatial support for product states σ0.

Grade 0.356 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Federico Tomás B. Pérez, Gabriela Wójtowicz, Martin B. Plenio

Figure

Instantaneous absolute error ΔZ0(t) and computational resource cost versus time for covariance PP, Hilbert--Schmidt PP across m=1,2,3, and tensor-network benchmarks on a 3×3×2 transverse-field Ising lattice.

Asks

How can Heisenberg-picture Pauli propagation be truncated reliably and stably during coherent many-body dynamics?

Before

Conventional Hilbert--Schmidt weight-based truncation and state-informed methods like xSPD discard components above weight m, losing target expectation value preservation and suffering from instability.

But

Product reference states σ0; requires exponential tail concentration Θr(g)(s)≤Cge2ℳ1(s)e−2κgr for certified sufficiency; rank-deficient states can suffer compatibility failures in covariance quotient geometry.

Tools

state-adapted generalized mean-field projections · covariance bilinear form · adaptive hierarchical-basis Krylov evolution · Lieb-Robinson bounds · Rényi-2 operator-space entanglement entropy

Abstract

The Heisenberg picture can make quantum many-body simulation efficient when evolved observables admit compact operator representation within low-dimensional structures. Conventional Pauli-string propagation and truncation techniques exploit this structure, but in coherent Hamiltonian dynamics their error control is often heuristic and their stability can be poor. We introduce a state-adapted Krylov framework based on geometric generalized mean-field projections of many-body observables onto low-body operator subspaces. The resulting dynamics approximate expectation values, do not extend spatial support beyond that prescribed by Lieb-Robinson bounds, and compress high-body correlations onto their state-relevant low-body representatives rather than simply discarding them. We derive necessary operator-entanglement obstructions to low-body representation and conditional sufficient bounds on representation and dynamical errors involving nonstabilizerness and controlled high-body tails. Numerical benchmarks show improved, stable finite-m hierarchies and simulations on large three-dimensional lattices, establishing a scalable state-adapted alternative to conventional Heisenberg-picture weight-truncation of Pauli strings.

item.title: Sparse-Blossom Decoding in o(1) Time
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Parallel sparse blossom decodes an O(d)-round syndrome extraction window on a distance-d rotated surface code in average parallel runtime bounded by exp⁡[O((log⁡log⁡d)2)], yielding o(1) average parallel runtime per round.

Grade 0.351 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling” · Ryo Mikami, Hayata Yamasaki

Figure

Event counts per shot per syndrome extraction round plotted against code distance d∈{9,13,…,49}, demonstrating that parallel sparse-blossom runtime per round decreases with increasing d at low physical error rates.

Asks

Can minimum-weight perfect matching decoding via sparse blossom be parallelized with an exact correctness guarantee and a runtime per round that scales as o(1)?

Before

Decoding time per round scaled as O(d2.34) in sequential sparse blossom, requiring O(d3.34) total latency for a d-round window (Higgott and Gidney 2023).

But

Circuit-level local stochastic error model below a finite threshold pth, with finite-size numerical comparisons assuming negligible parallelization overhead.

Tools

parallel sparse blossom · hierarchical error clustering · minimum-weight embedded matching · rotated surface code simulation

Abstract

Matching-based decoding is widely used in quantum error correction, and accelerating it is key to enabling fast and scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoding provides rigorous guarantees for error suppression, while sparse blossom enables its practical implementation at modest problem sizes. However, the runtime of existing sparse-blossom implementations unavoidably increases with problem size, motivating a rigorous parallelization framework that guarantees correctness and a runtime shorter than the syndrome-extraction timescale. Here, we present such a framework and prove that the resulting parallel sparse-blossom algorithm produces the same correction as the original, non-parallel sparse blossom. For the rotated surface code with code distance d and physical error rates below a finite threshold, we prove that the average parallel runtime of decoding for O(d) rounds of syndrome extraction is upper bounded by a quasi-polylogarithmic function of d. For a d-round decoding window, this implies that the average parallel runtime per round is o(1). We also perform numerical simulation to identify conditions under which the parallel runtime per round decreases with increasing code distance. These results suggest that increasing code distance need not lead to longer parallel decoding times, providing a foundation for scalable parallel matching-based decoding.

item.title: Testing and Diagnosing Parameter Miscalibration in Probabilistic Error Cancellation via Direct Fidelity Estimation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — DFE overlap Y≡Tr⁡(ρρ~) and purity 𝒫≡Tr⁡(ρ~2) of PEC-mitigated state ρ~ serve as hardware witnesses and directional diagnostics: consistent underestimation yields Y≤1 and 𝒫≤1, while consistent overestimation yields Y≥1 and 𝒫≥1.

Grade 0.340 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Francesc Sabater, Tristan Kraft, Carlos A. Riofrío, Barbara Kraus

Figure

DFE overlap Tr⁡(ρ~ρ) plotted against assumed depolarizing parameter p~e for N=50 qubits and s=50,100,150 gates. The curve crosses 1 exactly at the true parameter pe=0.02, being <1 for underestimated p~e and >1 for overestimated p~e.

Asks

How to test whether the noise parameters used in Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) are accurate directly on hardware, and diagnose whether they are overestimated or underestimated?

But

Requires positive Pauli fidelities (>1/2 identity coefficient) and absence of hybrid miscalibration; overestimation directionality for Y in arbitrary circuits holds perturbatively under a nondegeneracy condition, while purity condition 𝒫 holds non-perturbatively.

Tools

Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) · Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) · Two-copy purity estimator · Classically simulable surrogate circuits

Abstract

Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) is a standard technique for mitigating noise in quantum computations, but its unbiasedness relies on accurate knowledge of the underlying noise parameters. In practice, these parameters are inferred from experimental data and may be inaccurate. We introduce a protocol that tests PEC parameter consistency on hardware by applying Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) to the effective mitigated state. The resulting DFE overlap serves not only as a witness of parameter miscalibration but, under appropriate conditions, also reveals whether the PEC parameters have been overestimated or underestimated. We establish this behavior for arbitrary circuits under global depolarizing noise and for Clifford circuits under general Pauli-stochastic noise. For arbitrary circuits subject to Pauli-stochastic noise, the underestimation result holds generally, while the corresponding overestimation result is established perturbatively for sufficiently small consistent miscalibrations under an additional nondegeneracy condition. We further show that the purity of the effective mitigated operator provides a more general diagnostic, allowing the miscalibration direction to be identified for arbitrary circuits and arbitrary parameter deviations. Finally, we describe a two-copy PEC procedure for measuring this quantity and show that, together with the DFE overlap, it determines the Hilbert-Schmidt distance from the ideal state. The sampling overhead incurred by our protocol is the same as that of PEC, and we discuss strategies to improve it.

item.title: Error Correction in a Distributed Quantum Computer
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Real-time distributed error detection and feedforward correction demonstrated across two trapped-ion quantum processors separated by ∼2 m. Stabilises logical qubit in a [[2,1,1]] repetition code and actively corrects arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state.

Grade 0.340 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · E. M. Ainley, A. Agrawal, T. Araki, A. R. Martínez, D. Main, E. Malinowski, J. A. Blackmore, S. Chen, P. Drmota, M. Mallweger, D. P. Nadlinger, R. Srinivas, S. C. Benjamin, G. Araneda, D. M. Lucas

Figure

Remote stabiliser measurement scheme and network qubit parity readout. Network qubit parity plotted against analysis pulse phase demonstrates syndrome discrimination between +1 and −1 eigenspaces of data-qubit pairs.

Asks

Can stabiliser measurements and quantum error detection/correction be performed across spatially separated quantum processors using photonic interconnects?

But

Interleaved recooling reduces entanglement generation rate from ∼100 s−1 to ∼10 s−1. Calibration drifts and gate phase offsets not fully captured in error budget.

Tools

trapped-ion processors (⁸⁸Sr⁺, ⁴³Ca⁺) · photonic interconnects · mixed-species geometric phase gates · real-time classical feedforward (TTL link)

Abstract

Building fault-tolerant quantum computers with large numbers of logical qubits requires both scalable hardware architectures and error-correcting codes that make efficient use of physical qubits. Photonic interconnects address both of these challenges by allowing the physical qubits to be distributed across multiple processors while providing the non-local connectivity necessary to implement resource-efficient codes such as high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. A key requirement for realising this architecture is the ability to perform stabiliser measurements between remote processors, which has not previously been demonstrated experimentally. Here we report the first experimental demonstration of distributed quantum error detection and correction. We generate entanglement between network qubits in two separate trapped-ion processors and use it to perform remote syndrome measurements on data qubits. We first realise a distributed [[2, 1, 1]] repetition code, detecting phase-flip errors on a logical qubit encoded across the two modules in real time and suppressing logical errors. We then combine these mid-circuit syndrome measurements with real-time feedforward to actively correct arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state. These results provide an experimental foundation for quantum error correction (QEC) across modular quantum architectures.
